questions.stem:
Ruby says: 'Our school should send reports to parents online instead of on paper. It would save the school a lot of money on paper and printing.'
Which statement, if true, most weakens Ruby's argument?

options.A: The online report system would cost the school more each year than it now spends on paper and printing.
options.B: Some parents prefer to read reports on paper.
options.C: The price of paper has gone up this year.
options.D: Several nearby schools already send reports online.

questions.explanation: Ruby's only reason is saving money. If the online system costs more, the switch would not save money at all.

distractors.B: this might be a reason not to switch, but it doesn't touch her reason (saving money)
distractors.C: this strengthens her argument

questions.stem:
If more than 20 mm of rain falls overnight, the river track is closed in the morning. Whenever the river track is closed, the ranger puts a sign at the car park.
Mia: 'There is no sign at the car park this morning, so not more than 20 mm of rain fell overnight.'
Jon: 'The river track is closed this morning, so more than 20 mm of rain must have fallen overnight.'
If the information above is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.explanation: Mia ✓: heavy rain → track closed → sign. No sign means the track isn't closed, so there can't have been heavy rain. Jon ✗: the rules say heavy rain closes the track, not that it is the only reason for a closure.

distractors.B: the track could be closed for another reason, such as a fallen tree
distractors.C: Jon reverses the rule
distractors.D: Mia works backwards correctly from 'no sign'

questions.stem: At a market, 3 shells can be swapped for 2 beads, and 5 beads can be swapped for 4 feathers. How many shells are needed to get 16 feathers?
questions.explanation: 16 feathers = 4 lots of 4 feathers = 4 × 5 = 20 beads. 20 beads = 10 lots of 2 beads = 10 × 3 = 30 shells.

distractors.A: that is the number of beads
distractors.B: multiplied 16 by 3 and divided by 2
distractors.D: worked one exchange the wrong way round

questions.stem:
Research shows that people who sleep less than 8 hours a night tend to feel more tired the next day.
Kai: 'I only slept 6 hours last night, so I will definitely feel tired today.'
Lea: 'Ravi feels tired today, so he must have slept less than 8 hours last night.'
If the information above is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.explanation: 'Tend to' describes what usually happens, not what always happens. Kai ✗: he might not feel tired. Lea ✗: Ravi could be tired for another reason, even after a long sleep.

distractors.A: Kai treats a tendency as a certainty
distractors.C: tiredness can have other causes

questions.stem:
Birds' nests that are left alone by people are rarely abandoned. Most nests that are disturbed by people are abandoned.
Grace: 'This nest was disturbed by people, so it will be abandoned.'
Hugo: 'That nest was abandoned, so it must have been disturbed by people.'
If the information above is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.explanation: 'Most' and 'rarely' don't mean 'always' and 'never'. Grace ✗: a disturbed nest is likely, not certain, to be abandoned. Hugo ✗: undisturbed nests are rarely abandoned, but it can still happen.

distractors.B: 'most' isn't 'all'
distractors.C: 'rarely' isn't 'never'

questions.stem:
Councillor Rao says: 'We should turn the old concrete car park on Mill Street into a grassy park. This will reduce the flooding in Mill Street, because grass soaks up rainwater and concrete does not.'
Which statement, if true, most strengthens the councillor's argument?

options.A: Grassy parks are popular with families with young children.
options.B: Some streets in the town flood even though they have no car parks nearby.
options.C: Grass soaks up less water when the ground is already wet.
options.D: Most of the water that floods Mill Street runs off the car park during storms.

questions.explanation: If the car park is the main source of the flood water, replacing its concrete with grass targets the cause directly.

distractors.A: a reason to like parks, not about flooding
distractors.B: this suggests other causes of flooding, so it weakens rather than strengthens
distractors.C: this weakens the argument

questions.stem:
All the students in the debating team are also in the library club. Some members of the library club are in Year 6. No Year 5 students are in the library club.
Ana: 'None of the Year 5 students is in the debating team.'
Ben: 'Some members of the debating team are in Year 6.'
If the information above is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.explanation: Ana ✓: debaters are all in the library club, and no Year 5 student is in the library club, so no Year 5 student debates. Ben ✗: the Year 6 library club members might all be outside the debating team.

distractors.A: the Year 6 members might not be debaters
distractors.C: Ben's conclusion doesn't have to be true

questions.stem:
Tom says: 'Our team lost our last three games, and Jake was away for all of them. Jake will be back for the next game, so we will win.'

options.B: The next team they play is weaker than the last three teams.
options.C: The team has never lost a game when Jake has played.
options.D: Jake being away was the reason the team lost.

questions.explanation: Tom concludes that Jake's return will turn losses into a win. That only works if Jake's absence was what caused the losses.

questions.stem:
There are 25 students in a class. Each student voted for exactly one of three excursions: the zoo, the museum or the beach.
Pia: 'At least one of the excursions must have got 9 or more votes.'
Tom: 'At least one of the excursions must have got 8 or fewer votes.'
If the information above is true, whose reasoning is correct?
questions.explanation: Pia ✓: if every excursion had 8 or fewer, the total would be at most 24, but there are 25 votes. Tom ✓: if every excursion had 9 or more, the total would be at least 27, which is more than 25.

distractors.A: Tom's reasoning also works: 3 × 9 = 27 is more than 25
distractors.B: Pia's works too: 3 × 8 = 24 is less than 25
distractors.D: try the largest and smallest possible totals

• Dee does not sit next to Cal.

Who sits in the middle seat?
questions.explanation: Try both ends for Eve and test the arrangements. Every arrangement that fits all the clues (Eve, Cal, Ben, Ava, Dee) has Ben in the middle.

distractors.D: place Eve first, then test where Cal can go

questions.stem: In a game, an easy puzzle earns 3 coins and a hard puzzle earns 5 coins. Lena wants to buy a hat (25 coins), boots (22 coins) and a cape (17 coins). She must solve at least 2 easy puzzles and at least 2 hard puzzles. What is the fewest puzzles she can solve to afford all three items?
questions.explanation: She needs 25 + 22 + 17 = 64 coins. Hard puzzles give more, so use as many as possible: 2 easy (6 coins) leaves 58, which needs 12 hard puzzles (60 coins). 2 + 12 = 14. Check 13 puzzles: the most coins is 2 × 3 + 11 × 5 = 61, not enough. So 14.

distractors.B: not the fewest
distractors.C: 13 puzzles earn at most 61 coins

Which statement, if true, most strengthens Mr Tan's conclusion?

• Customer 1: used FASTFIX. Repair lasted a year? (unknown)
• Customer 2: used FASTFIX? (unknown). Repair lasted a year.
• Customer 3: did not use FASTFIX. Repair lasted a year? (unknown)
• Customer 4: used FASTFIX? (unknown). Repair did NOT last a year.
Which two pieces of missing information must be found out to test the company's claim?
questions.explanation: The claim can only be shown false by a customer who used FASTFIX and whose repair did NOT last. Customer 1 used it, so we need to know if the repair lasted. distractors.A: Customer 2's repair lasted, so it can't break the claim either way

distractors.D: Customer 3 didn't use FASTFIX, so the claim says nothing about them

questions.stem:
Five runners, P, Q, R, S and T, finish a race with no ties.
• P finished ahead of Q.
• R and S finished one straight after the other (in either order).
• T did not win.
How many different finishing orders are possible?
questions.explanation: Treat R and S as one block (2 ways to arrange inside it). That gives 4 'items' to order: 24 orders × 2 = 48. Half have P ahead of Q: 24. Now remove those where T is first: with T first, the block and P, Q fill the rest: 3! × 2 ÷ 2 = 6. So 24 − 6 = 18.

distractors.B: forgot to remove the orders where T wins
distractors.C: halved too many times
distractors.D: forgot that P must be ahead of Q

questions.stem:
Someone broke the classroom window. Exactly ONE of these four students is lying.
Amy: 'It was Bob or Cara.'
Bob: 'It wasn't me.'
Cara: 'It was Dan.'
Dan: 'Cara is lying.'
Who broke the window?
questions.explanation: Cara and Dan contradict each other, so one of them is the liar, which means Amy and Bob are both telling the truth. Bob: it wasn't Bob. Amy: it was Bob or Cara, so it was Cara. Check: Cara's statement ('It was Dan') is the one lie, and Dan ('Cara is lying') is telling the truth. Exactly one lie ✓.

distractors.A: count how many statements would be true
distractors.C: count how many statements would be true
distractors.D: count how many statements would be true

questions.stem:
Each card has a shape on one side and a colour on the other. The rule is: 'If a card has a triangle on one side, it is red on the other side.' The four cards show:
  TRIANGLE     CIRCLE     RED     BLUE
Which cards must be turned over to check whether the rule has been broken?
questions.explanation: The rule is broken only by a triangle with a colour that isn't red. Turn the TRIANGLE (is the back red?) and the BLUE card (is there a triangle on the back?). A RED card can have anything on the back, and a CIRCLE isn't covered by the rule.

distractors.A: a red card with a circle on the back doesn't break the rule
distractors.B: a blue card might hide a triangle
distractors.D: the red card can't break the rule

questions.stem:
30 tables at a party are all the same size. Each has 1, 2 or 3 vases of flowers on it, and there are 62 vases altogether. There are twice as many tables with two vases as tables with three vases.
How many tables have two vases?
questions.explanation: Call the number of three-vase tables t. Then there are 2t two-vase tables and 30 − 3t one-vase tables. Vases: (30 − 3t) + 2 × 2t + 3t = 30 + 4t = 62, so t = 8. Two-vase tables: 2 × 8 = 16. (Check: 6 + 2 × 16 + 3 × 8 = 62 ✓.)

distractors.B: that is the one-vase tables
distractors.C: that is the three-vase tables
